**Hindsight on the builder's own practice.** Test the first cut on the real desktop before

## Scope & Idea Clarity

**What landed:** The cycle's scope came from one sentence of yours, "make sure we are ready for any
user", with two named worries: text over files on a full desktop, and Mods & Config being new and
loose. The ux-polish scan turned that into 37 anchored rows, each with a file and line, scored on
user trust. That is a scope with a user in it (someone with a full desktop, someone opening Mods
& Config for the first time) and cuts that followed from the score.

**What to tighten:** `docs/scope.md` still describes the June Windows rebuild. The Mac app has no
scope of its own beyond the per-item specs. One page naming the Mac's user and its cuts would have
saved the "what is our actual concern" turn, because the layer-order ask was a scope fact, not a
polish item.

## Requirements Thinking

**What landed:** Run 2's items carried acceptance criteria that tests could pin: the plate and the
clicks default differ for new and existing installs (D1, D2, both pinned); the hex fields save on
commit and refuse a bad value (D8); the vocabulary change renames strings and nothing stored (D3).
The worker that declined half of item 13 did it with two test citations, which is requirements
thinking at the right moment.

**What to tighten:** `docs/prd.md` carries no requirement for the Desk layer at all, and the
click-layer requirement was discovered in conversation: "meeting links still clickable", then
"files still movable". Both were knowable up front. The next Desk feature deserves one line of
acceptance per thing the user can still do after it ships.

## Technical Decisions

**What landed:** The click layer runs the plates, the mouse-through switch and the click dispatch
on one element list (`DeskClickLayer.elements`), with a point-by-point test against the hit test,
so the three cannot disagree. The DeskLayer window level is derived from `CGWindowLevelForKey`, not
a magic number, and the test pins it between the desktop and the icon layer. Run 1's six shared
helpers (digest, stamp, JSON read, owner-only write, result files, process runner) were byte-for-
byte refactors with the stamps and hashes proven unchanged.

**What to tighten:** Icon-awareness was ruled out on one probe (Finder scripting returns no
positions on a sorted desktop). That is the right call for this release and should be written
down where the next person will look, with the Accessibility route named, so the question is not
re-opened from scratch. `docs/spec.md`'s Mac section is the place.

## Plan vs. Reality

**What landed:** Both Cart runs closed at 100 percent merged, 16 and 14 items, with the build,
the full test suite and the selftest run per item and again before each merge. Drift was handled
in the ledger: the ADR format, the "By Seat" rename reaching older cards, the hex commit rule.

**What to tighten:** Three release runs for one release. The first two failed on Apple's staple
service; the third succeeded with the retry that should have existed before. The draft's notes
came out empty because the ship commit retitled the CHANGELOG heading that `docs/mac-release.md`
step 10 says to rename only after the release, and the publish landed on a placeholder tag, which
no step checked for. One of those was in the runbook and not followed; the other was not in it.
The keystone now names both, the runbook's publish step now says to confirm the tag, and the
memory file keeps the heading rule where the ship commit is written.

## How You Worked

**What landed:** You shaped every turn that mattered. "just the portables for now" scoped the
mods question in four words; "naw the windows agent can handle it" kept the wall where it belongs;
"2" answered a two-option diagnostic without a word wasted. You approved releases explicitly and
only when asked, and you tested the dev build on your own desktop twice when the tests were green.

**What to tighten:** The two misses on the click layer were caught by you on the Mac, not by me
before handing it over. On the next Desk change, ask for the real-desktop check before the design
is approved, not after. That is a practice note for both of us.

## Your Goals

The profile on file holds no written goals. The goal stated in this cycle was "ready for any
user", and asked whether it landed, the builder's answer was yes. Evidence it was reached: a new install gets

an existing install changes nothing until a toggle. Evidence of the remainder: the run report

## Reflection

Builder's answer, asked after the autonomous run: nothing surprised him. "This system works."

Agent's read on what surprised: the real concern was a layer-order option, and it surfaced only
after a 14-item polish run had shipped around it. The scan read the symptom (text over files) and
proposed readability; one sentence from you named the cause. Scans find rough patches; they do not
find what the owner wants the surface to be. Ask that question first next time.
